title: fighting slop with slop — Vaibhav Gupta, Boundary

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 86%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: BAML is a programming language and developer tool designed for software engineers working with AI agents. The talk is fundamentally about building infrastructure — language design, CLI tooling, type systems, cross-language bridges — for the developer community adopting agent-driven development.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: The talk directly addresses coding assistant workflows: agents generating code from scratch, eliminating human code reviews, agent-first tooling replacing grep with semantic search, and managing the quality of agent-generated code through detection layers and compiler guarantees.

summary:
Vaibhav Gupta, Co-Founder and CEO of Boundary, presents "fighting slop with slop," a philosophy for managing AI-generated code quality developed while building BAML, an agent-first programming language. He defines slop as "any code you don't read" and argues it is inevitable and ever-growing. His eight-person team ships a production programming language with no code reviews, no AI tool standardization, and mandatory parallel work.

The strategy has two layers. First, hard invariants: a tiny architecture.md containing only stable compiler-layer rules unchanged for months, design docs backed by Markdown with Slack notifications for social accountability, and CLI tools that enforce dependency graph invariants. Second, a messy detection layer: agents continuously generate BAML programs from scratch while other agents inspect Claude transcripts to find hallucinations, errors, and inefficiencies, enabling data-driven language design via AB-testing tool-call counts and error rates.

Gupta then argues that winning detection battles is insufficient because foundational tools like TypeScript are themselves broken—designed for human, not agent, productivity. BAML addresses this from first principles: execution traces with near-zero overhead, semantic code search replacing grep, every function as a standalone CLI command, cross-platform binary bundling targeting WASM, inferred error types with compiler-proven exhaustive handling, and type-safe cross-language function calls (Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java) including lambdas, generics, and closures. The type system becomes the absolute center of truth. He frames code as "a matter of trust"—we don't use ML code blindly because underlying systems lack rigidity. His closing challenge urges building sloppy tools, making processes robust, and reimaging foundational systems: "we need a new Git, a new database, a new programming language."
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk are deeply interconnected: the engineering practices (hard invariants, CLI enforcement, type-safe boundaries, inferred error types) provide the stable foundation that makes aggressive AI agent usage viable, while the AI concepts (agent-driven transcript inspection, AB-testing via tool-call metrics, agent-first tooling) represent the messy layer that operates on top of those invariants. BAML as a programming language is the convergence point—its compiler-enforced type safety creates the 'rigidity' that Gupta argues is necessary to trust ML-generated code, while its agent-first design (every function as CLI, semantic code search, cross-language type safety) makes agents more productive. The 'fighting slop with slop' philosophy ties them together: you accept that AI generates unread code, but you contain it with hard engineering invariants below and messy AI detection above. Without the engineering concepts, the AI practices would be uncontrolled chaos; without the AI concepts, the engineering practices would be traditional software engineering with no acceleration. The talk argues this synthesis is the only viable path forward as agent-generated code grows, and extends the argument to foundational systems (Git, databases, languages) that must be rebuilt for an agent-first world.
temporalContext: The video was published on 2026-07-31. As of the research date (2026-08-23), BAML was at version 0.16.0 (BAML Language, canary 2026-08-12) and 0.225.0 (BAML v0, 2026-07-31), confirming the project is pre-1.0 but under active nightly-build development. Boundary was founded in January 2023 (YC W23 batch), and the talk describes approximately two years of active language development. The talk was given during a period of rapid growth in agent-driven software engineering tooling, with BAML's GitHub stars roughly doubling from ~5k (August 2025) to ~9.1k (August 2026). The practices described—no code reviews, agent-driven detection, compiler-enforced type safety—represent an early-stage, experimental approach to agent-first development that may evolve significantly before BAML reaches 1.0.
takeaways: 'Slop is just any code you don't read' — it is inevitable and any codebase will only accumulate more over time.
Hard invariants (architecture.md, enforced design docs, CLI dependency checks) provide a stable base that doesn't change for months, letting messy AI detection operate on top.
Agents inspecting other agents' transcripts can detect hallucinations, errors, and inefficiencies automatically, enabling data-driven language design without writing code.
TypeScript and JavaScript bake in slop at the foundational layer because they were designed for human productivity, not agent productivity.
Agent-first tooling replaces multi-step grep with single semantic tool calls that return function descriptions, docstrings, source code, and usage locations.
Every BAML function becomes a standalone CLI command; all tools can bundle into one cross-platform binary targeting Windows, Mac, Linux, and WASM.
Error types are inferred without writing code, enabling compilers to prove exhaustive error handling—division by zero is guaranteed handled or the code won't build.
BAML functions are callable from Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, and Java with full type safety, including lambdas, generics, and closures across language boundaries.
The type system is the absolute center of truth that prevents invariants from entering the codebase—'code is a matter of trust.'
Gupta's closing challenge: build sloppy tools yourself, make systems robust, and reimagine foundational layers—we need new Git, new databases, and new programming languages.

concepts.name: Agents inspecting agent transcripts for hallucination detection
concepts.explanation: Using AI agents to automatically inspect other agents' full Claude conversation transcripts to find hallucinations, errors, and inefficiencies that human review would miss.
concepts.importance: Core mechanism of the 'fighting slop with slop' detection layer—automated quality monitoring of agent-generated code without human code review.

concepts.name: AB-testing language features via tool-call metrics
concepts.explanation: Using agent tool-call counts and error rates as quantitative metrics for evaluating language design decisions, enabling data-driven feature comparison.
concepts.importance: Transforms language design from intuition-based to empirical, allowing small teams to iterate at a pace previously requiring tens of thousands of man-hours.

concepts.name: Agent-first tooling design
concepts.explanation: Designing developer tools from the ground up for AI agent consumers rather than human consumers—single semantic tool calls replace multi-step grep workflows, every function is guessable.
concepts.importance: Represents a paradigm shift where tooling ergonomics are optimized for agent productivity rather than human readability, fundamentally changing how development infrastructure should be built.

concepts.name: Fighting slop with slop (cheap agents detecting cheap agent output)
concepts.explanation: The philosophy of using cheap, messy AI agents to detect problems in cheap, messy AI-generated code, accepting that slop is inevitable and weaponizing it as a detection mechanism.
concepts.importance: The talk's title concept and central thesis—reframes the relationship between AI quality and AI quantity, arguing that messy detection is sufficient when paired with hard invariants.

concepts.name: Agent productivity vs human productivity as language design goal
concepts.explanation: TypeScript and JavaScript were designed to balance correctness with human productivity; BAML is designed for agent productivity, recognizing that foundational language choices determine where slop accumulates.
concepts.importance: Identifies the root cause of why agent-generated code in TypeScript produces slop—the language itself was not designed for agent consumers.

concepts.name: ML-generated code trust via compiler rigidity
concepts.explanation: The principle that ML-generated code can be trusted only when underlying systems have sufficient compiler-enforced rigidity, extending the trust we already place in compilers to agent-generated code.
concepts.importance: Bridges the gap between AI code generation and production safety—argues that the solution is not better AI but more rigid foundations that constrain AI output.

concepts.name: Rejection of AI tool standardization
concepts.explanation: The deliberate choice not to standardize which AI tools or models the team uses, instead creating model-agnostic standards (architecture.md) that any agent can follow.
concepts.importance: Contrasts with common enterprise AI governance approaches—argues that standardizing the invariant layer is more effective than standardizing the tools.

concepts.name: Claude transcripts as first-class inspection artifacts
concepts.explanation: Using full Claude conversation transcripts as the primary inspection surface for detecting agent errors and inefficiencies, treating transcripts as quality monitoring data rather than ephemeral conversations.
concepts.importance: Elevates agent conversation logs to a first-class engineering artifact, enabling systematic quality analysis that human code review cannot replicate at scale.

concepts.name: Agent-driven quality detection layer
concepts.explanation: A systematic approach where AI agents serve as an automated quality detection layer, continuously probing generated code for hallucinations and inefficiencies that human review would miss.
concepts.importance: Replaces human code review with a scalable, always-on detection mechanism that can operate at the volume and speed of agent-generated code.

concepts.name: Continuous agent-generated program synthesis for testing
concepts.explanation: Agents constantly generate BAML programs from scratch as a testing mechanism, with the generated programs serving as both test cases and quality detection probes for the language itself.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a novel use of AI code generation—not for production code but as an automated fuzzing and regression testing harness for language design.

concepts.name: Slop taxonomy (unread code)
concepts.explanation: Gupta defines 'slop' as any code you don't read, framing it as an inevitable and ever-growing phenomenon in codebases that must be managed rather than eliminated.
concepts.importance: This is the central framing concept that motivates the entire talk's two-layer strategy of hard invariants plus messy AI detection.

concepts.name: Hard invariants as architectural foundation
concepts.explanation: Using stable, slowly-changing documents (architecture.md) containing only months-stable compiler-layer rules as a model-agnostic foundation that any AI agent can understand and follow.
concepts.importance: Provides the stable base layer that allows messy AI-driven code generation and detection to operate safely on top without corrupting core architecture.

concepts.name: Design docs with social accountability
concepts.explanation: Replacing Notion/GitHub with Markdown-backed design docs that notify a Slack channel on every update, creating social pressure for quality, with a mandatory must-be-read rule since 'code can be slop, writing cannot.'
concepts.importance: Ensures the human-readable specification layer maintains higher quality standards than generated code, preventing specification slop from compounding code slop.

concepts.name: CLI dependency graph enforcement
concepts.explanation: CLI tools that visualize and enforce dependency graph invariants, catching when agents add leaky dependencies across module boundaries that violate architectural rules.
concepts.importance: Automates invariant enforcement that would otherwise require human code review, making the no-code-review practice viable.

concepts.name: Elimination of code reviews in favor of agent-driven detection
concepts.explanation: The radical practice of removing human code reviews entirely, relying instead on agent-driven transcript inspection and compiler-enforced type safety to catch issues.
concepts.importance: Challenges a foundational software engineering practice and demonstrates an alternative quality model viable when compiler rigidity and agent detection are strong enough.

concepts.name: Execution traces with near-zero overhead
concepts.explanation: Built-from-scratch execution traces showing time spent per program part with effectively zero performance cost, enabling autonomous bug-finding and optimization by agents.
concepts.importance: Replaces line-by-line human code reading with automated observability, a key enabler of the no-code-review model and agent-first development.

concepts.name: Semantic code search replacing grep
concepts.explanation: Agent-first tooling where a single tool call returns a function's description, docstrings, source code, and usage locations, replacing multi-step grep/Ripgrep workflows.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how tooling designed for agent consumers rather than human consumers can eliminate entire classes of multi-step workflows, increasing agent productivity.

concepts.name: Every function as a CLI command
concepts.explanation: BAML automatically exposes every function as a standalone CLI command with type-safe arguments, making functions type-safe, deterministic, and guessable for agents.
concepts.importance: Eliminates the need for agents to grep for function signatures or guess argument types, reducing hallucination surface area in agent-generated code.

concepts.name: Cross-platform binary bundling (WASM, Windows, Mac, Linux)
concepts.explanation: All CLI tools bundle into a standalone cross-platform binary targeting Windows, Mac, Linux, and WASM, ensuring deterministic execution everywhere.
concepts.importance: Eliminates environment-specific variability that causes agent failures, making the entire toolchain reproducible and agent-friendly.

concepts.name: Inferred error types
concepts.explanation: Error types are inferred without developers writing code, so a divide function knows it throws division-by-zero and calling functions know too, without manual annotations.
concepts.importance: Removes a major source of human error and slop in error handling, making exhaustive error coverage automatic rather than dependent on developer discipline.

concepts.name: Compiler-enforced exhaustive error handling
concepts.explanation: The compiler proves whether errors are handled or not, guaranteeing exhaustive coverage—if an API guarantees no throws, the system catches violations at build time.
concepts.importance: Eliminates whole classes of runtime errors that agents typically introduce through repeated try/catch nesting and console.log fallbacks.

concepts.name: Type-safe cross-language function calls
concepts.explanation: BAML functions are callable from Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, and Java with full type safety, including lambdas, generics, and closures across language boundaries.
concepts.importance: Enables incremental adoption without requiring full codebase rewrites, addressing the limitation that asking everyone to rewrite would 'lose the war on slop.'

concepts.name: Type system as center of truth
concepts.explanation: The type system serves as the absolute source of truth that prevents invariants from entering the codebase—'the type system never lies'—replacing documentation and architecture files as the definitive reference.
concepts.importance: Makes compiler rigidity the enforcement mechanism for all architectural invariants, enabling trust in agent-generated code without human verification.

concepts.name: Code visualization with semantic boundaries
concepts.explanation: Code visualization tools with expandable semantic boundaries that let humans opt into specific sections rather than reading everything, paired with per-file execution traces.
concepts.importance: Replaces linear code reading with selective semantic exploration, making human oversight scalable even as agent-generated code volume grows.

concepts.name: CI/CD adoption analogy for foundational system changes
concepts.explanation: Drawing an analogy to CI/CD adoption: teams slow down for three months while adding it, then move much faster, as a model for the cost-benefit of adopting agent-first foundational systems.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete mental model for adoption cost, addressing the practical objection that replacing foundational tools is too expensive.

concepts.name: Data-driven language design via agent feedback
concepts.explanation: Using agent-generated programs and transcript analysis to AB-test language features by comparing tool-call counts, error rates, and correct outcomes—designing a language without writing test code.
concepts.importance: Shows how AI agents can serve as an automated testing and evaluation harness for language design, dramatically reducing the human effort required to build production-quality compilers.

sections.title: Fighting slop with slop — team practices and philosophy
sections.summary: Gupta introduces his team's radical practices: no code reviews, no AI standardization, parallel work. They build a programming language needing correctness. He defines slop as any code you don't read and frames the talk as a war against it.

sections.title: Standards and invariants — architecture.md
sections.summary: Instead of standardizing AI tools, the team uses architecture.md so any model can understand it. It must be tiny and contain only things stable for months or years, like compiler layers. Agents are told to talk to at least one person.

sections.title: Design docs with notifications and social accountability
sections.summary: Guiding principle: 'code can be slop, writing cannot.' A custom design doc tool replaces Notion/GitHub, backed by Markdown and CLI scripts. A Slack integration notifies a channel on every update. A final rule requires design docs to actually be read.

sections.title: CLI tools that catch where things break
sections.summary: A dependency graph visualization tool with semantic boundaries lets the team watch the codebase change. CLI tools guarantee invariants can't be broken, catching when agents add leaky dependencies. Architecture hasn't changed in 3-4 months.

sections.title: Agents reading agent transcripts
sections.summary: Agents constantly generate BAML programs from scratch. Humans and other agents inspect full Claude transcripts to find what was good, bad, or inefficient. Features can be AB-tested by comparing tool-call counts, error rates, and correct outcomes.

sections.title: Data-driven systems and the cost advantage
sections.summary: Data-driven language design is possible without writing code. Eight people built a programming language in under two years—traditionally requiring tens of thousands of man-hours. Millions of tokens make it stable.

sections.title: Attacking the foundational layer — TypeScript slop
sections.summary: Despite winning detection battles, Gupta predicts losing the war because foundational layers are broken. TypeScript balances correctness and human productivity, not agent productivity. JavaScript→CoffeeScript→TypeScript layered fixes on a broken base.

sections.title: Execution traces and code visualization from first principles
sections.summary: BAML offers a new way to understand code: visualization with expandable semantic boundaries and execution traces showing time spent per program part with near-zero overhead. Per-file tracing lets Claude find bugs and optimize code autonomously.

sections.title: Agent-first tooling — semantic code search beyond grep
sections.summary: Gupta asks what agent-first tooling looks like. Instead of Ripgrep returning raw matches, a single tool call could describe a function, return its docstrings, source code, and all usage locations. He emphasizes 'the code is always the source of truth'—docs and architecture files may lie, but code cannot.

sections.title: Every function as a CLI command and cross-platform binaries
sections.summary: Every BAML function is immediately available as a CLI command (e.g., 'add' with A and B parameters). All CLI tools can be bundled into a standalone binary targeting any architecture including WASM. Everything becomes type-safe, deterministic, and guessable—agents don't need to grep. Builds target Windows, Mac, and Linux.

sections.title: Fixing JavaScript error handling from first principles
sections.summary: Gupta attacks errors as a deeper sin of JavaScript. Agents nest try/catch repeatedly and give up with console.log. In BAML, error types are inferred without writing code: divide knows it throws division by zero, and calling functions know too. The compiler proves exhaustive handling—no unknowns, no guessing. If an API guarantees no throws, the system catches violations.

sections.title: Code as a matter of trust and compiler rigidity
sections.summary: Gupta frames code as a matter of trust. We don't use ML-generated code blindly because underlying systems lack rigidity. Compilers already do invisible work we trust; the same trust principle must extend to agent-generated code.

sections.title: BAML across languages — type-safe cross-language calls
sections.summary: Recognizing that asking everyone to rewrite code would lose the war, BAML functions are accessible from Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, and Java with full type safety. Async variants come free. Lambdas, generics, and closures pass across language boundaries. The type system becomes the absolute center of truth preventing invariants from entering the codebase.

sections.title: Closing philosophy and call to action
sections.summary: Gupta closes by arguing complex systems can be built without code reviews, with parallel work and unstandardized AI use—but only with thoughtful engineering practices. An engineer built a partial C compiler in BAML. He draws a CI/CD analogy: adoption slows teams for 3 months, then they move faster. 'This is the least amount of slop your codebase will ever have.' He urges building sloppy tools, making systems robust, and for the bravest, reimagining foundational layers: 'we need a new Git, a new database, a new programming language.'

organization.name: Boundary
organization.summary: Boundary is a privately held technology company headquartered in Seattle, WA, founded in 2023 as a Y Combinator W23 batch company. The company builds and maintains BAML (Basically A Made-up Language), a Turing-complete, open-source (Apache-2.0) programming language designed for software written by AI agents and humans. BAML features TypeScript-like syntax with a Rust-like type system (no 'any' or unchecked casts), typed and statically analyzed errors with exhaustive pattern matching, green threads with colorless concurrency like Go, built-in test and eval framework, native LLM functions, baml describe for AST-aware code discovery, baml run for CLI execution of any function, and cross-language SDK generation for Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, C#, C++, Swift, and WASM. The GitHub repository (BoundaryML/baml) has approximately 9.1k stars, 486 forks, 3,755 commits, and is primarily written in Rust (70.7%). The company has approximately 9 employees and $625K in total funding from seed rounds led by Y Combinator. Vaibhav Gupta is Co-Founder and CEO. The YC company page confirms: 'Boundary is building BAML -- a programming language to build AI agents.'

technologies.label: BAML Programming Language
technologies.summary: BAML (Basically A Made-up Language) is a Turing-complete, open-source programming language designed for software written by AI agents and humans. It features TypeScript-like syntax with no 'any' or unchecked casts, typed errors with exhaustive pattern matching, green threads with spawn/await, native LLM functions, cross-language SDK generation, and built-in CLI tooling (baml describe, baml run). The language is built from first principles for agent productivity rather than human productivity, addressing what Gupta identifies as foundational slop baked into TypeScript and JavaScript. An 8-person team built the language in under two years using data-driven, agent-assisted development practices without human code reviews.
technologies.role: Central and pervasive — BAML is the product, the platform, and the demonstration surface for every technical concept in the talk. The entire presentation revolves around building BAML and the engineering practices developed around it.

technologies.label: Agent-Driven Code Quality Detection
technologies.primary: Agent transcript inspection for hallucination and error detection
technologies.summary: A technique where AI agents continuously generate programs from scratch while other agents inspect full Claude conversation transcripts to detect hallucinations, errors, and inefficiencies automatically. This enables data-driven language design by AB-testing features via tool-call counts and error rates, replacing traditional human code review with automated, always-on agent-driven quality monitoring. An 8-person team used this approach to build a production programming language in under two years, work that would traditionally require tens of thousands of man-hours. The technique represents the 'messy detection layer' in the talk's two-layer strategy of hard invariants plus messy AI detection.
technologies.role: Defines the talk's central thesis and title — 'fighting slop with slop' — as the messy AI detection layer that replaces human code review with automated agent-driven quality monitoring, enabling radical team practices like no code reviews and no AI tool standardization.

technologies.label: Type-Safe Cross-Language Interop & Compiler-Enforced Error Handling
technologies.primary: Type-safe cross-language function calls with inferred error types and exhaustive compiler proofs
technologies.summary: BAML provides type-safe cross-language function calls where functions written in BAML can be invoked from Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, and Java with full type safety, including passing lambdas, generics, and closures across language boundaries. Error types are inferred automatically without developer annotation, and the compiler proves exhaustive error handling at build time — if an API guarantees no throws, violations are caught during compilation. The type system serves as the absolute center of truth with no escape hatches ('any' or unchecked casts), preventing invariants from entering the codebase. This addresses the practical adoption problem: teams don't need to rewrite existing code fully, enabling incremental integration of compiler-enforced safety into existing codebases.
technologies.role: Key enabler for incremental adoption and the trust foundation for agent-generated code. Demonstrated through concrete examples: BAML calculate function called from Python with full type safety, Python lambdas passed across language boundaries, and compiler-proven exhaustive error handling for division-by-zero.

technologies.label: Agent-First Tooling & Execution Observability
technologies.primary: Agent-first developer tooling with semantic code search, CLI-per-function, and zero-cost execution traces
technologies.summary: A suite of agent-first developer tools built into BAML that optimize for agent productivity rather than human productivity. Key capabilities include: semantic code search (single tool calls returning function descriptions, docstrings, source, and usage locations instead of raw grep matches), automatic CLI exposure of every function with type-safe arguments, cross-platform binary bundling targeting Windows/Mac/Linux/WASM, and execution traces with near-zero performance overhead enabling autonomous agent-driven debugging and optimization. These tools exemplify the talk's thesis that foundational tooling must be redesigned for agent consumers — 'code is always the source of truth' but tools should make that source maximally accessible to agents in minimal calls.
technologies.role: Demonstrated as the concrete realization of agent-first design principles — replacing grep with semantic search, manual CLI scaffolding with automatic function-to-CLI translation, environment-specific builds with cross-platform bundling, and line-by-line human code reading with zero-cost execution traces.

resources.title: Boundary: Building a Programming Language at Agent Speed with AI-First Development Practices
resources.why: Most comprehensive external secondary source confirming the talk's content. Independently verifies: (1) 8 engineers built a production-ready language in under two years, (2) no code reviews / no AI tool standardization / mandatory parallel work, (3) agents inspecting Claude transcripts for errors and inefficiencies, (4) inferred error types with exhaustive compiler proofs, (5) partial C compiler built in BAML the day before the talk, (6) cross-language calls from Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java with lambdas, generics, and closures. Also provides critical assessment noting the approach works partly because Boundary builds developer tooling/compiler where formal methods are particularly effective.

resources.title: ai that works: No Vibes Allowed - Building Design Docs with AI | BAML Podcast
resources.why: First-party content from Boundary elaborating on the design doc system, Slack notifications, and slop management philosophy described in the talk. Provides additional context on the team's approach to AI-assisted development, including the systematic workflow of specification refinement, codebase research, implementation planning, and phased execution using Claude. The 400,000+ line codebase size mentioned provides scale context for the talk's claims about managing agent-generated code.
